lead: Ponchon-Savarit steps binary stages on an enthalpy-composition diagram instead of a y-x diagram. It drops constant molar overflow, so it handles unequal latent heats and heats of mixing: two enthalpy curves and one difference point per section carry the material and energy balances together.
prereq: You need: 4.1 VLE for equilibrium tie lines, 4.4 operating lines, and basic enthalpy balances from thermodynamics.

sections.h3: Two enthalpy curves and a fixed point

blocks.text: McCabe-Thiele assumes that each mole of vapour condensed sends one mole of liquid down, which needs equal latent heats and no heat losses. Ponchon-Savarit drops that assumption and keeps the energy balance.

The diagram has two enthalpy curves. H is the enthalpy of saturated vapour in kJ per mole of mixture, plotted against vapour mole fraction y. h is the enthalpy of saturated liquid in kJ per mole of mixture, plotted against liquid mole fraction x. Both x and y refer to the more volatile component. The vertical gap H − h at equilibrium is the latent heat of vaporisation; it need not be constant.

A difference point replaces the operating line. For the rectifying section it is Δ<sub>D</sub>, at abscissa x<sub>D</sub> and an ordinate H<sub>ΔD</sub> fixed by the reflux ratio; every rectifying operating line passes through it.

Take an envelope round the condenser and the top of the column. Vapour V₁ from the top tray, with y₁ = x<sub>D</sub> for a total condenser and enthalpy H₁, is condensed; L₀ = RD returns as reflux and D leaves, both as liquid with enthalpy h<sub>D</sub>. The condenser removes Q<sub>C</sub> = V₁(H₁ − h<sub>D</sub>). Only these top values are needed to place the difference point:
H<sub>ΔD</sub> = h<sub>D</sub> + Q<sub>C</sub>/D = H₁ + R(H₁ − h<sub>D</sub>)
blocks.where: H<sub>ΔD</sub> is the ordinate of the rectifying difference point (kJ/mol); H₁ is the enthalpy of the saturated vapour leaving the top tray at y₁ = x<sub>D</sub> (kJ/mol); h<sub>D</sub> is the enthalpy of the saturated reflux and distillate liquid (kJ/mol); Q<sub>C</sub> is the condenser duty (kJ/h); R = L₀/D.

blocks.text: Δ<sub>D</sub> = (x<sub>D</sub>, H<sub>ΔD</sub>) is a construction point, not a tray. It sits above the H curve, higher for a larger R. Every rectifying operating line passes through it: the passing streams x<sub>n</sub> (liquid down from tray n) and y<sub>n+1</sub> (vapour up from tray n + 1) lie on one straight line through Δ<sub>D</sub>.

items: Plot H against y and h against x on the same axes, with tie lines from the equilibrium data.
Mark Δ<sub>D</sub> at (x<sub>D</sub>, H<sub>ΔD</sub>), directly above the distillate composition.
Top tray: with a total condenser y₁ = x<sub>D</sub>, the point (x<sub>D</sub>, H₁) on the H curve.
Follow the tie line from y₁ down to the h curve: this is x₁, the liquid leaving tray 1.
Draw the line from Δ<sub>D</sub> through (x₁, h₁) and extend it to cut the H curve: the cut is y₂, the vapour rising to tray 1.
Repeat tie line and operating line until x passes the feed composition, then switch to Δ<sub>B</sub>.

blocks.text: The lever rule on each operating line gives the internal reflux ratio: L<sub>n</sub>/V<sub>n+1</sub> = (H<sub>ΔD</sub> − H<sub>n+1</sub>)/(H<sub>ΔD</sub> − h<sub>n</sub>). When the H and h curves slope, this ratio changes from tray to tray, which is exactly what McCabe-Thiele cannot show.

sections.h3: Stripping point and the McCabe-Thiele limit

blocks.text: The stripping section has its own difference point Δ<sub>B</sub> at x<sub>B</sub>, with ordinate H<sub>ΔB</sub> = h<sub>B</sub> − Q<sub>B</sub>/B, where Q<sub>B</sub> is the reboiler duty and B the bottoms flow. It lies below the h curve. A balance round the whole column puts Δ<sub>D</sub>, the feed point F = (z<sub>F</sub>, h<sub>F</sub>) and Δ<sub>B</sub> on one straight line: once Δ<sub>D</sub> is placed, Δ<sub>B</sub> is where the line from Δ<sub>D</sub> through F crosses the vertical x = x<sub>B</sub>. Stripping operating lines are drawn through Δ<sub>B</sub>.

McCabe-Thiele is the special case of horizontal curves, H = H<sub>V</sub> and h = h<sub>L</sub> with constant gap λ = H<sub>V</sub> − h<sub>L</sub>. Then H<sub>ΔD</sub> = H<sub>V</sub> + Rλ, and the lever rule gives L/V = (H<sub>ΔD</sub> − H<sub>V</sub>)/(H<sub>ΔD</sub> − h<sub>L</sub>) = Rλ/[(R + 1)λ] = R/(R + 1) on every tray: constant molar overflow. The operating line returns as With H<sub>V</sub> = 50, h<sub>L</sub> = 20 kJ/mol and R = 2, for example, H<sub>ΔD</sub> = 50 + 2(30) = 110 kJ/mol and L/V = 60/90 = 0.667.

blocks.where: y is the vapour mole fraction on the McCabe-Thiele operating line; x is the liquid mole fraction; R is the reflux ratio; xD is the distillate mole fraction. This is the rectifying line of McCabe-Thiele.

blocks.text: Columns whose curves are nearly flat and parallel can use McCabe-Thiele. Large or unequal latent heats, heats of mixing and wide boiling ranges (ammonia-water, concentrated acids) need Ponchon-Savarit.

Δ<sub>D</sub>, the feed F and Δ<sub>B</sub> = (0.05, −26.6) lie on one line.

spec.aria: Enthalpy against composition. A falling vapour line near 40 to 50 kilojoules per mole and a falling liquid line near 16 to 20, a difference point high at x 0.95 and 89.1, another low at x 0.05 and minus 26.6, a dashed line joining them through the feed point at 0.40, and three tie lines with operating lines near the right-hand end.

examples.question: Take H = 50 − 10y and h = 20 − 4x kJ/mol, so the latent heat falls from 30 to 24 kJ/mol. With α = 2.5, x<sub>D</sub> = 0.95, R = 2.0 (total condenser), saturated-liquid feed at z<sub>F</sub> = 0.40 and x<sub>B</sub> = 0.05, place Δ<sub>D</sub> and Δ<sub>B</sub>, step three trays from the top, and compare L/V with McCabe-Thiele.
steps: H<sub>ΔD</sub> = 40.5 + 2.0(40.5 − 16.2) = 40.5 + 48.6 = 89.1 kJ/mol, so Δ<sub>D</sub> = (0.95, 89.1). Condenser duty per mole of distillate: 89.1 − 16.2 = 72.9 kJ/mol.
Line from Δ<sub>D</sub> through (0.8837, 16.47) has slope (89.1 − 16.47)/(0.95 − 0.8837) = 1096 kJ/mol per unit x. It cuts H = 50 − 10y at y₂ = 0.9061 (H₂ = 40.94). McCabe-Thiele gives 0.9058.
Repeat for trays 2 and 3 (table): y₃ = 0.8474 and y₄ = 0.7800, against 0.8461 and 0.7764 from the McCabe-Thiele line at the same x.
Internal reflux by the lever rule: L₁/V₂ = (89.1 − 40.94)/(89.1 − 16.47) = 0.663, then 0.658 and 0.653, all below R/(R + 1) = 0.667 and falling.

Δ<sub>B</sub>: the feed point is (0.40, h<sub>F</sub> = 18.4). The line from Δ<sub>D</sub> through F has slope (89.1 − 18.4)/(0.95 − 0.40) = 128.5; at x = 0.05 it reaches 18.4 − 128.5 × 0.35 = −26.6 kJ/mol. So Δ<sub>B</sub> = (0.05, −26.6) and the reboiler supplies h<sub>B</sub> − H<sub>ΔB</sub> = 19.8 + 26.6 = 46.4 kJ per mole of bottoms.
examples.answer: Δ<sub>D</sub> = (0.95, 89.1 kJ/mol) and Δ<sub>B</sub> = (0.05, −26.6 kJ/mol). The internal L/V drifts from 0.663 to 0.653 instead of staying at 0.667, so each vapour is a little richer than McCabe-Thiele predicts; over a full column the stage count differs.
examples.check:
a = 2.5; xD = 0.95; R = 2.0
H = lambda y: 50 - 10*y
h = lambda x: 20 - 4*x
Hd = H(xD) + R*(H(xD) - h(xD))
print(round(Hd, 1))
y = xD
for n in range(3):
    x = y/(a - (a - 1)*y); hx = h(x); m = (Hd - hx)/(xD - x)
    y = (50 - hx + m*x)/(m + 10)
    print(round(y, 4), round((Hd - H(y))/(Hd - hx), 3))
print(round(h(0.4) - (Hd - h(0.4))/(xD - 0.4)*0.35, 1))

traps: Putting Δ<sub>D</sub> on a saturated curve. It is fixed by x<sub>D</sub> and the condenser balance and lies above the H curve.
Using H and h per mole of one component. They are per mole of mixture; a mole of mixture changes composition.

Reading H<sub>ΔD</sub> as the condenser duty. H<sub>ΔD</sub> = h<sub>D</sub> + Q<sub>C</sub>/D, so the duty per mole of distillate is H<sub>ΔD</sub> − h<sub>D</sub> (72.9 kJ/mol in the worked example).
Placing Δ<sub>B</sub> above the h curve. It normally lies below because the reboiler adds heat.
Locating Δ<sub>B</sub> independently of Δ<sub>D</sub>. For a given feed, Δ<sub>D</sub>, F and Δ<sub>B</sub> are collinear; Δ<sub>B</sub> is where that line meets x = x<sub>B</sub>.

quiz.q: What is plotted on the two curves of a Ponchon-Savarit diagram?
quiz.a: The upper curve is the saturated-vapour enthalpy H against vapour mole fraction y; the lower curve is the saturated-liquid enthalpy h against liquid mole fraction x. Both are per mole of mixture, and tie lines join equilibrium pairs.

quiz.q: Write the formula for H<sub>ΔD</sub> when H<sub>V</sub> and h<sub>L</sub> are constant.
quiz.a: H<sub>ΔD</sub> = H<sub>V</sub> + R(H<sub>V</sub> − h<sub>L</sub>), where R = L/D is the reflux ratio.

quiz.q: Why does Ponchon-Savarit not need the constant molar overflow assumption?
quiz.a: It carries an enthalpy balance alongside the material balance, so the liquid and vapour flows may change from tray to tray as the H and h curves dictate. McCabe-Thiele fixes them, which needs equal latent heats and no heat loss.

quiz.q: Use H<sub>V</sub> = 50 kJ/mol, h<sub>L</sub> = 20 kJ/mol, x<sub>D</sub> = 0.95 and R = 3.0. Find H<sub>ΔD</sub>.
quiz.a: H<sub>V</sub> − h<sub>L</sub> = 50 − 20 = 30 kJ/mol. R(H<sub>V</sub> − h<sub>L</sub>) = 3.0 × 30 = 90 kJ/mol. H<sub>ΔD</sub> = 50 + 90 = 140 kJ/mol. The point is (0.95, 140 kJ/mol).

quiz.q: What happens to Δ<sub>D</sub> and the rectifying operating lines as R increases at fixed x<sub>D</sub>?
quiz.a: Δ<sub>D</sub> moves up, since H<sub>ΔD</sub> = H₁ + R(H₁ − h<sub>D</sub>). Lines from the higher point cut the H curve nearer each tie-line end, so each tray does more and fewer trays are needed, while the condenser duty per mole of distillate, H<sub>ΔD</sub> − h<sub>D</sub>, grows.

quiz.q: In the worked example the feed is F = 100 kmol/h. Find D, the condenser duty and the internal L₁/V₂ on tray 1.

beyond: Not for the exam. Simulators solve the same enthalpy balances numerically, so Ponchon-Savarit is now a visual check. Search "enthalpy-composition diagram" and "Ponchon-Savarit construction".
